en: In order to refute a relation that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*), the author of the *Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti* says: "Dependence," and so forth.
For dependence is indeed a relation; but when [the related entities] are already established, what dependence could there be?

Therefore, no entity whatsoever possesses a relation in reality. Dependence, which is the state of being reliant on another—that is relation—would have to belong either to a related term that is already established or to one that is not yet established. Since that which is unestablished has the nature of non-existence, it cannot be a real entity.
[Regarding] relation: even when the related entity is established, what dependence [could there be]? "None at all" means there is no relation.
Even for that which is established, something remains unestablished; thus, even upon the establishment of that [unestablished part], there is no dependence.

It is not tenable, because it does not transcend the conceptual constructions of the faults regarding the states of being established or unestablished. Furthermore, the two forms of being established and unestablished do not exist for a single entity. Precisely because of this, there is no dependence of one thing upon another, whether it be established or otherwise. Therefore, in reality, there is no relation between any entity and a real object.
Therefore, there is no negation of that which is constructed by conceptualization, because it lacks substantial reality.
For a relation is indeed a conjunction of forms, and that [conjunction] requires duality; how could that exist?
Therefore, for things that are essentially distinct, there is no relation in reality. 2

[V.2] If it is argued that connection (*sambandha*) is indeed the fusion of forms (*rūpaśleṣa*) and not dependence (*pāratantrya*), that is not so. For when there is duality of the two related entities, how could that fusion of forms—which is characterized by identity of nature (*svabhāvaikātmya*)—possibly exist? It could not exist at all, even if those two were identical.
Since there is no existence of two related entities, what relation can there be, given that a relation resides in both?

This might be argued: "Conjunction is not a single nature; rather, it is contiguity. Let it be so. What is the refutation? It is merely that contiguity is the absence of an interval; thus, it would be a real entity.

There would be no connection. Furthermore, if uninterruptedness (*nairantarya*) were the connection, why is separatedness (*sāntaratā*) not accepted as a connection? For in both cases, there is no difference in the persistence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the two related entities.
Even [concepts] such as "attainment" (*prāpti*) are included within the meaning of uninterruptedness, and thus need not be mentioned separately. Since...

Thus, even a relationship characterized by the fusion of form does not exist; therefore, for all entities that are distinct by nature, there is no relationship in reality other than that which is superimposed through conceptual construction.
For dependence is indeed a relation; how can that which is non-existent depend?
And how can an existent thing, which is independent of everything else, depend?
[v.3] Now, if it is argued that dependence is a relation and not a physical conjunction, even in this case, regarding the other—
If that which is dependent were related by virtue of its dependence, would it depend while existing or while not existing?

If it does not exist, how can that which is non-existent depend? For a thing whose own nature has not been produced, dependence cannot be its property; thus, what relationship could there be between them?

And how could that entity, which is entirely free from expectation and independent of the intrinsic nature of all things, depend [on anything], such that there would be a relation of dependence? The remainder should be explained as being like [the case of] dependence on another.
If it is argued that the relation between two things exists because of their connection with a single [third] thing, then [that relation must exist] between those two.

"What is the relationship? And there would be an infinite regress; likewise, there would be no cognition of the relationship. [Verse 4ab] "Lest this fault should occur," [it is argued that it arises] from the connection of two related things with a single [third thing]—either through a quality (*guṇa*) called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), which is a distinct entity, or through something that is not a distinct entity.

Because of a connection with a real entity (*vastubhūta*) that is inexpressible by means of a property (*dharma*), if a relation is admitted—then, in the case where [the related entities] are not distinct from one another, the two relata would be merely imagined as isolated;
thus, there would be no relation whatsoever. Furthermore, from that relation, the two relata would not be...

And because of the identity [of the relation] with its relata, even for that which is a real entity yet inexpressible, it logically cannot escape the alternatives of being either a different thing or not a different thing. In the case of it not being a different thing, there would be neither a relation nor any related entity whatsoever.
Or, let there be a relation that is a different thing or something else; nevertheless, in both cases, [the same difficulty persists].

What is the connection? What is the connection between the two related entities by means of that single [third] entity? It is not so. Just as there is no connection between two related entities due to the aforementioned faults, so too by this [third entity] there is no connection between the two related entities. Otherwise, [if it were otherwise], there would be a connection between the two related entities in isolation.
What is the negation regarding the relation?

Furthermore, if a relation is accepted on the basis of its connection with a single object, then both the relation and the related entities must likewise possess a connection with that same single object. Likewise, the relation—

Furthermore, because one must again accept a relation between those two [terms] for the sake of a single unified meaning, there would be an infinite regress. Consequently, a relation of a single unified meaning could never be established anywhere. In the absence of such a relation, there would be no cognition of a relation anywhere; thus, the cognition of a relation does not follow from a real entity.

While the locus [of inherence] exists, if one were to postulate a relation in some cases even without a connection to a single object, then there would be no relation between the first two relata either, because they too would be connected through a single object.
Furthermore, the fault in the case of a relation between two things taken alone has already been stated. By this, [the argument regarding] isolation...
The postulation of further properties for the horse and so forth is also refuted.
Those two entities and everything else distinct from them—each abides in its own nature;
thus, these entities are inherently unmixed, yet conceptual construction mixes them together. (5)

[Verse 5] Since even this conceptualization of a relation is not superior, therefore those two entities intended as being related, as well as that other thing called the "relation"—all these, as previously described, abide in their own selves; that is, they abide each in its own respective intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Therefore, they are unmixed.

Entities are by their very nature unconnected with themselves. If it is asked, "How then are they designated through various connections when their forms depend upon them?", [the answer is: in reality, no connection exists at all.
It is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that mixes those entities, even though they are unmixed. That [construction] too...
It arises as if displaying forms dependent on something else due to some cause;
and following that very [form], expressive words denoting actions and factors of action are joined together for the purpose of conveying the distinctions of states (bhāva). (6)
[V.6] And following that very conceptual construction, persons associate expressive words— those denoting actions and those denoting factors of action— and designate them,
thinking "this denotes an action" and "this denotes a factor of action," for the purpose of cognizing the distinctions between states of being.

The differentiation of entities is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); it is for the purpose of conveying that [exclusion], and not, however, a real relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*),
nor even a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between those two, because they do not exist simultaneously.
How can that which is characterized by aversion be established in relation to that which is free from aversion? How can there be a relationship?

(7) If it is argued that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) will then be established as the relationship, that is not so; for how could even the causal relationship, as a relationship, be established at all? It is not established at all.
Of what nature is it? It is "dual-abiding" (dviṣṭha). What is the reason? Because of the non-simultaneity of those two, cause and effect.

For instance, when there is the cause, the effect is not; or at that time, the cause is not [simultaneous with] it, because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable at the same time. This is also because even non-momentary things lack existence.
Furthermore, even the examples cited by the proponents of non-momentariness—namely, the relation of cause and effect or simultaneous existence—are inappropriate here;

for there exist no two simultaneously occurring entities that possess real substantiality such that a relationship could subsist between them. And how can there be the state of being related when the entities themselves do not coexist? Certainly not. Bu-...
Having been explained through meditation, the relationship would be constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
An entity existing sequentially in one place is indifferent to others;
since that [entity] exists even in the absence of those [others], the relationship does not reside in a single locus. (8)

[V.8] It is also untenable to claim that a relation exists sequentially in either the cause or the effect. For even if it were to exist sequentially, a relation—being a single entity existing in one place within either the cause or the effect—would be indifferent to the other; if it resides in the cause, it would be independent of the effect.

The claim that "while existing as an effect, it is independent of its cause" implies that [the two] exist sequentially; thus, there is no relation between them. Whatever is indifferent toward something cannot have a relation with it.
A sequential causal relationship exists merely through a single occurrence, because even in the absence of that [cause], the [effect] may still exist.
Because there exists an entity called "relation" (*sambandha*) even when cause and effect are mutually absent;
for if one of those two were to depend upon the other, this [relation] would function in the other.

For that which is beneficial must be dependent; and how can that which is non-existent be beneficial? [Verse 9] Lest this fault should arise, if one of those two—the effect or the cause—is dependent upon the other, whether it be the effect or the cause, then that relation would occur sequentially.

If it is maintained that [the effect] exists [at the time of the cause] because it is desired [by the agent], then it must be something beneficial to that which desires it. Why? Because only something beneficial can be desired, and nothing else.
If you argue that "that which is desired must be something beneficial," then how can that which is non-existent be beneficial at the time of the cause?

That which is called the "effect" does not exist at the time of the effect, and that which is called the "cause" does not exist [at the time of the cause]; thus, it cannot provide assistance due to its lack of capacity.

If the relationship of cause and effect between those two were due to their connection with a single object, then the relationship of cause and effect would also obtain between the left and right horns of an animal, due to their connection with the duality [of being two horns]. (10)
Furthermore, if the causal relationship between those two things intended as cause and effect were to arise from the reason of their connection with a single object,
then a causal relationship would also obtain between the left and right horns of a cow by virtue of their connection with the number known as "duality" and so forth. Yet this is not accepted.

Let it not be so even in other cases; for by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the definition would over-extend] due to relations such as priority, posteriority, or horn-ness. For a relation is indeed something that resides in two [relata], and there is no definition of it other than this.

If connection is the relation between existence and non-existence, or the state of cause and effect, [then it is not established]. If it is argued that a connection does not arise from a mere single entity, but rather from a single entity characterized as "connection," that is not so; for some entity must reside in both [relata].

As for the relation: since it is not possible to establish a definition of that relation as something other than the object itself which connects two objects, by means of which a distinction such as number and so forth could be determined for it.

If causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is a connection (*yoga*) characterized by existence and non-existence— that is, a connection for which the qualifiers (*upādhi*) or specifications are the existence that occurs when something exists and the non-existence that occurs when it does not exist— then it is not every kind of connection [that constitutes causality].
Are not those very two—existence and non-existence—which serve as the limiting adjuncts of conjunction, what constitutes causality here?
If it is argued that they are distinct, then surely this term "causality" depends upon the one who employs it.
(12) Thus, those two states of existence and non-existence, which are the limiting adjuncts of conjunction, are themselves what constitute causality here.

Why not? Because it would involve the postulation of a relation for something non-existent and fruitless. If it is argued that this might be so because there are many designata—namely, "existence when [the cause] exists" and "non-existence when [the cause] does not exist"—and these must be expressed by a single term denoting a single object, such as "causality," then it is improper to have multiple objects; thus, existence and non-existence do not [constitute a single relation].

The relationship of cause and effect is thus maintained. But surely, this word depends upon a person who employs it; therefore, because it relies on an employer, whatever word he uses in a particular way, that word expresses exactly that—thus, even in multiple instances, there is but a single usage of the term. This is simply not a solution.
Seeing one thing when another is not seen, and not seeing it when that other is not seen, people infer the effect even without informants.
Therefore, it is logical that the cause-and-effect relationship consists precisely of those two: existence and non-existence. For this reason:

Observing one thing regarded as the cause when that which is called the effect—which, though meeting the conditions for perception, was previously unobserved—is seen; and observing that he did not see it when the [cause] was not seen;
he follows the thing regarded as the effect and understands: "This arises from that," even without [explicit verbal instruction].
People [understand] from speakers that "this arises from that"; thus, people understand it even without a speaker.

Furthermore, it is a mere report to say that they follow [the meaning] through convention (*saṅketa*). For indeed, even in the case of convention, one does not apprehend anything other than existence and non-existence. Therefore, when the cognition of X occurs upon the cognition of Y, X is the referent of Y.

For example, just as when one perceives a white cloth, there is the whiteness resulting from the perception of the white; and since one who perceives existence and non-existence perceives the relation of cause and effect, existence and non-existence are the objects of the perception of causality, and nothing else.

It might be argued as follows: existence and non-existence are the means of proof (*sādhana*), while causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is the object to be proven (*sādhya*). If it is something else, why is its nature not specified? Its nature, then, is the relationship between that which is produced and that which produces. Is there a difference in meaning from a mere change in name such that this is stated in this way? For indeed, the relationship between the produced and the producer—
The relationship between the produced and the producer, the relationship between effect and cause, and so forth, are synonyms.
This is because the cognition of an "effect" is impossible apart from perception and non-perception.
Furthermore, the terminology such as "effect" has been introduced here for the sake of brevity. (14)

Therefore, since perception and non-perception are impossible for the cognition of an effect apart from the existence and non-existence of the object— because they consist in the manifestation of the object by the subject— the term "effect" and so forth is used here with respect to existence and non-existence, lest people employ such an extensive string of words at every step.

It is established for the sake of simplifying conventional usage. Even that description of the attainment of an effect based on the presence of that [cause] is merely a designation of the object of a convention, just as the cognition of a cow is based on the dewlap and other such features. (15)

[Verse 15] There is no causal relation other than through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). If it is not otherwise, how is that [causal relation] established by means of existence and non-existence? From the mark (*liṅga*) that "when this exists, that exists," there is the cognition of its effect; that is, when something exists and another exists, there is the cognition of that as its effect, which is further described as "this belongs to that."

"Effect and cause"—this is a designation for the objects of conventional usage. This description, which occurs because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, is merely a designation for the objects of the convention "effect and cause"; there is no difference in the actual object. How so? Just as there is the cognition of a cow from [the perception of] its dewlap and so forth; just as one says, "This is a cow, because it possesses a dewlap and so forth."
By this, the scope of the conventional usage of "cow" is demonstrated:
when a thing exists, that which is to exist comes into being; and the state of being a thing is simply its existence.
The relationship between cause and effect is well-established through perception and non-perception. (16)

[V.16] This might be the case: if existence and non-existence constitute the relationship of cause and effect, then causality and effectuality would both depend upon the existence and non-existence residing in both [the cause and the effect]. Otherwise, how could mere existence be either the cause or the effect? Furthermore, for you, neither existence nor non-existence belongs to that which exists or that which does not exist.
Is causality (kāryatva) or being a cause (kāraṇatva) located in both [the effect and the cause]? Or rather, would there be a relation of effect and cause?
That is not so. Even if it were located in both, causality consists in the presence and absence of the prior [cause] being qualified by the presence and absence of the subsequent [effect];
and the presence and absence of the subsequent [effect] being qualified by the presence and absence of the prior [cause].

The two states are "being an effect. For it is thus: when the entity (bhāva)—that which is to come into being and possesses the nature of coming into being—is present, the existence of that [entity] is the existence of what is considered the cause. Here too, the restriction "only when there is existence" implies the negative concomitance (vyatireka). And the state of being-to-come-into-being occurs only when the existence of what is considered the cause is present.

The status of being an effect for that which is considered an effect is well known through perception and non-perception as the relation of cause and effect. Since it is thus, existence and non-existence alone constitute causality; there is no other.
The scope of cause and effect has as its true meaning nothing more than this.
Conceptual constructions display objects as if they were composed of false entities.

(17) Therefore, these have only this much as their reality (*tattva*). Existence and non-existence are just this much; that object whose reality is precisely those two is "that which has only this much as its reality. That is the object.

Those conceptual constructions for which these [entities] have as their object a reality consisting of nothing more than this—what is it? They have as their seed nothing more than this, and they operate within the sphere of cause and effect. They present objects as if they were joined together, as if connected, though they are actually unconnected.
And because of such a joining, they are false objects.

If [the two] are distinct, what is the connection? If they are non-distinct, how can there even be a relationship of cause and effect? For if one thing exists, how could those two be both separated and joined?
[18] Why is a non-existent relation demonstrated by them, on account of which their objects would be false? Thus...

This is so because, in this regard, there are two possible conceptual alternatives: the related entities existing as cause and effect must be either different or non-different. If they are different, what kind of connection could there be between things that are different? None at all, because each is established in its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If, on the other hand, they are non-different, then what would even constitute the relationship of cause and effect in that which is non-different? It would be nothing.
Or rather, because there is no existence of that which is to be produced as something distinct from its cause; how, then, could there be a conjunction of two?
It might be argued: "There is no relation of either a distinct or a non-distinct entity taken alone; rather—"

"Because of the connection with that one called 'relation' (sambandha). Here too, while existence (bhāva) is being (sattā), how could two things regarded as cause and effect—which are distinct from another thing called "relation"—become conjoined? They certainly could not. That other thing called "relation" would itself have to be [the cause]; it is not, however, that very existence (tadbhāva).
Since there is no essential nature or conjunction with anything else, how could there be a real relation?
By this, all [cases] such as the conjoined (*saṃyogin*) and the inherent (*samavāyin*) have been considered;
and because they do not mutually benefit one another, such a thing cannot be a related entity. (19)

[Verse 19] "Conjunction, inherence, and so forth"— by the inclusion of "and so forth," [relations such as] owner and owned are meant. All this has been examined by the preceding section which refutes connection through the general argument that,
in reality, no relation characterized by conjunction and the like exists.
First of all, there is no relation of relatedness for things that are inherent, such as whiteness, which is an inherent quality in a cloth.

Because these two do not mutually assist one another—due to the absence of the relationship of producer and produced—the characteristic of inherence is not a relation; and such [a relation] does not exist where there is neither assistance nor being assisted.

How so? For that which is to be assisted by something else depends upon it, and that upon which it depends is related to it. But this is not the case for a white cloth, because their own natures are already established.
Furthermore, the relationship of container and contained does not exist between two things that are neither cause nor effect; and in the case of a cause-and-effect relationship...

The fault lies in that [assumption]. Since the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) exists only when there is a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), the postulation of a connection between "white" and "cloth" is also incorrect. For indeed, no worldly relation of locus and located exists between those two. And if the relation of locus and located were characterized by the producer and the produced, it would apply to the universal and its possessor.
There could be no relationship characterized by inherence between two things that do not stand in a mutual relation of benefactor and beneficiary;
for even in the case of the production of an effect by some inherent cause, [such a relationship would be impossible].
In that case, this [whole] would not be the inherent cause (samavāyin), because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

It might be argued: "There exists some inherent cause which produces the effect known as the composite whole; therefore, it is not unrelated due to a lack of assistance. But even if the effect is produced in such a way...

When something is accepted as an inherent cause (samavāyin), it is not an inherent cause at that time, because at the moment of production the effect is not yet accomplished and thus the two do not co-inhere; even when the effect is accomplished, the cause has vanished; and if it has not vanished, there can be no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between the two when they are already co-present.
Or, let there be some inherent cause; however, it is not so because of production from that cause. Why?
Because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since even a potter and the like would incur the status of being related [to the pot] due to its production [from them].
This would hold even if there were no mutual benefit between those two, whether in the case of inherence or in another relation.
If the universe were the relation, it would be an inherent (*samavāyin*) relation between each other.

[Verse 21] Now, if it is argued that this fault must not occur, then even if there is no mutual assistance between those two inherent relata, and even if there is no assistance from those two related things to the inherence, [the latter remains] because of its eternity.

If a relation is asserted between that [substance] and those two [qualities], or even in some other case where there is no mutual benefit, then the entire universe—the whole world—would be mutually inherent despite being unconnected to one another; but this is not so. Therefore, such a relation does not exist under the view that there is either benefit or lack of benefit.
There is no other possibility. By this, the two conjoined things are also refuted;
since they are not even desired to produce conjunction, they are therefore not conjoined.

Furthermore, their status as possessors of conjunction (*saṃyogitā*) has been refuted because it would entail their being subject to action (*karma*) and so forth, and because their persistence has already been explained. Moreover, since conjunction is an effect produced by those two [substances],

if they were to possess the state of being possessors of conjunction (*saṃyogitā*) due to its production, then even when the production of conjunction is thus accepted, it follows from that very cause— the production of conjunction— that...

Those two are not possessors of conjunction (*saṃyogin*). What is the reason? Because it would follow that they are possessors of action (*karman*) and so forth. If, by virtue of producing a conjunction, one were a possessor of conjunction, then action (*karman*) would also be a possessor of conjunction. For in this way, a conjunction is held to be produced by the action of either one or by the action of both. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) itself would also be a possessor of conjunction.
It might be argued that this [disjunction] is indeed accepted as being produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja*).

If it is claimed that its status as a "conjoined" entity does not arise from the production of conjunction, but rather from its stabilization (*sthāpana*), that is not correct. For stability has already been refuted; since there is a relationship of producer and produced between the stabilizer and the stabilized, there is no other form of stability.
In the *Pramāṇavārttika*, this has been refuted:
"That which is the substratum of conjunction and so forth arises as either capable or incapable;
for it is contradictory for that which has a permanent, capable nature to be deficient in such capacity. (23)

[Verse 23] If the cognition of conjunction and so forth occurs even in the absence of actual conjunction and so forth, then the form that belongs to two things when they are separated would also belong to them when they are conjoined; and likewise, the form that belongs to two things when they are conjoined would also belong to them when they are separated, as well as when they are stationary or moving. Why, then, does the cognition of conjunction and so forth not occur [in those cases]? But it is not so.

If it is argued that conjunctions, disjunctions, and motions are the causes for the cognition of conjunction and so forth, we say no, because the same objection applies equally. For you as well, why is there not an inherence of conjunction and so forth in that which is already divided and so forth, since its form is identical?

If it is argued that conjunction and disjunction do not arise because there is no action (*karman*) to produce them, then, this being the case, why should action itself not also have those [conjunction and disjunction] as its causes? This is difficult to answer. Therefore, you must say this:
that which has the form of being previously separated and so forth is unfit [to be a cause], whereas that which exists subsequently in the substratum of conjunction and so forth...

It arises as gold. What is the reason? Because it is contradictory for that which possesses a nature capable of being joined with eternal conjunction and so forth to be deficient in those [qualities];
thus, its deficiency in conjunction and so forth is a contradiction. I too must say this very same thing regarding that which is devoid of conjunction and so forth.
Thus, let its nature, which is expressed by the term "capacity," be defined;
what is the use of other [factors] such as division, conjunction, motion, or going?
(24) Therefore, let the nature of this object, which is denoted by the word "capacity," be defined.

What is the use of other imagined [motions] such as going and so forth, which are fruitless at that time, given that [motion] is already accounted for by conjunction, disjunction, action, and sound? Nothing at all. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), [other qualities] such as conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority are intended.

Even though those [actions such as going] exist, because the relation "belonging to that" is not established, this distinction of intrinsic nature is appropriate for things that arise at every moment.
(25) Why? Because, even though those [actions] such as going exist as mere conceptual constructs, the relation "belonging to that" [is not established].

Because [the cause] is unestablished. Since dependence and so forth are in every way refuted as a relation, and since this relation—whether conjunction or disjunction—is not established as its action, how can there be a designation based upon it? Just as [there is no designation] by means of actions and so forth belonging to one thing for another.

It does not become bound because of a lack of connection; likewise, [it is not bound] even by those things that are desired [as causes]. Since movement and so forth do not arise from a connection with karma and the like, therefore, for entities that arise at every moment, [the notion of movement] is due to successive conditions which serve as the basis for their continuous production and so on. Their own—

This distinction between entities—such as "conjoined," "disjoined," or "moving"—is logical only in a conventional sense, because for things that possess a stable, unitary nature, a relationship such as conjunction and so forth cannot be established. Thus, there is no real connection characterized by conjunction or the like; therefore, the intrinsic natures of all entities are without connection.
Peace.
The commentary on the *Sambandhaparīkṣā* is completed. The work of the teacher Devendrabuddhi. The book of Krauddhānvita.
